## Why pool at all

A single unit-root test on 20 or 30 annual observations has almost no power:
the Dickey–Fuller distribution is wide, and a root of 0.9 looks much like a
root of 1 over that span. Panel tests buy power by adding units instead of
years. *N* series of length *T* carry more evidence against a unit root than
one series of length *T*, provided the series bring *independent* evidence.

That proviso is the whole subject of this note. The extra power comes from
averaging, and averaging only helps when the things averaged are not the same
thing counted twice. Everything below is a consequence of asking what is being
averaged, and over what.

## 1. One null, three alternatives

Every test in `plm::purtest` and `plm::cipstest`, except Hadri's, shares one
null. Write each unit's ADF regression as

$$\Delta y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i y_{i,t-1}
  + \sum_{j=1}^{p_i} \gamma_{ij} \Delta y_{i,t-j} + \varepsilon_{it},
  \qquad \beta_i = \rho_i - 1.$$

The null is $H_0: \beta_i = 0$ for **every** *i*. The tests differ in what they
claim when they reject [@pesaran2015, pp. 818–820, eqs. 31.4–31.6]:

| | Alternative | In words | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| H₁ₐ | $\beta_i = \beta < 0$ for all *i* | one common stationary root | LLC, Harris–Tzavalis, Breitung |
| H₁b | $\beta_i < 0$ for $N_1$ units, $N_1/N \to \kappa > 0$ | a *share* of the panel is stationary | IPS, Fisher-type, CIPS |
| H₁c | $\beta_i < 0$ for a fixed number of units, $\kappa = 0$ | a *handful* is stationary | none |

H₁ₐ is strong: it says every unit reverts, and at the same speed. Few
economists believe that of 49 states or 170 regions, which is why the
heterogeneous alternative H₁b became the default after @im2003.

H₁c is the case no averaging test can see. With a fixed count of stationary
units, their signal is divided by an *N* that keeps growing. The
[simulation in the examples](index.qmd#sec-ur-alternative) shows it:
IPS power against two stationary series *falls* from 0.40 to 0.25 as *N*
goes from 10 to 90, while power against a 40% share rises to 1.

::: {.callout-important}
**The printed p-value does not carry the alternative.** `purtest` labels the
alternative "stationarity" for LLC and IPS alike, though LLC rejects towards
H₁ₐ and IPS towards H₁b. The alternative has to be written into the text by
hand, every time a panel unit-root result is reported.
:::

Remark 8 of @pesaran2015 [p. 820] sets the limit on that text. When *T* is
short — around 15 — a panel rejection is informative only "in an average
sense". It says the panel, taken as a whole, does not look like *N* random
walks. It does not say which units are stationary.

## 2. How the first generation builds a statistic

Each first-generation test runs the ADF regression above on every unit and
then combines the results. They differ only in *what* they combine.

| Family | What it combines | Tests in **plm** | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pooled | one $\hat\beta$ from all units stacked | `"levinlin"` | @levin2002 |
| Mean of *t* | the average of the *N* ADF *t* statistics | `"ips"` | @im2003 |
| Fisher | the *N* individual p-values | `"madwu"`, `"Pm"`, `"invnormal"`, `"logit"` | @maddala1999, @choi2001 |
| Reversed null | the *N* KPSS statistics | `"hadri"` | @hadri2000 |

**Pooled.** LLC stacks all units and estimates one $\beta$. Pooling only makes
sense if $\beta$ is common, so LLC's alternative is H₁ₐ by construction. The
pooled *t* is biased because each unit has its own intercept and lag
structure, and @levin2002 correct it with tabulated mean and variance
adjustments [@baltagi2021, pp. 340–343]. Harris–Tzavalis [@harris1999] and
Breitung [@breitung2000] are in the same family. Neither is in **plm**.

**Mean of *t*.** IPS averages the individual ADF statistics,
$\bar t = N^{-1}\sum_i t_i$, then standardises
[@baltagi2021, pp. 344–345]. Each unit keeps its own $\beta_i$, so the
alternative is H₁b. The unstandardised `tbar` is exact for fixed *T* but is
read against tabulated critical values, and only without lags.

**Fisher.** @maddala1999 combine the individual p-values instead of the
statistics: under the null, $-2\sum_i \ln p_i \sim \chi^2_{2N}$.
@choi2001 adds three variants. `"invnormal"` sums $\Phi^{-1}(p_i)$, `"logit"`
sums $\ln[p_i/(1-p_i)]$, and `"Pm"` standardises the Maddala–Wu statistic so
that it stays valid as $N \to \infty$. The Fisher family needs neither a
balanced panel nor equal lag lengths, which is why it runs on `EmplUK` where
LLC refuses [@baltagi2021, pp. 346–348].

A Fisher test is only as good as its p-values, and those come from the
non-standard Dickey–Fuller distribution. **plm** reads them off the response
surfaces of @mackinnon1996 through **urca** [@pfaff2008]. Without **urca** it
falls back to the older approximation of @mackinnon1994. On US house prices
the switch moves the Maddala–Wu p-value from 0.4292 to 0.4313 — visible in
the fourth decimal, irrelevant to a reading.

**Reversed null.** @hadri2000 tests the opposite hypothesis: every series is
stationary, against a unit root in at least one. It is the panel version of the
KPSS test [@kwiatkowski1992], an LM statistic averaged over units. Its value is
corroboration. When LLC, IPS and Maddala–Wu fail to reject a unit root and
Hadri rejects stationarity, two tests with opposite nulls point the same way.
That is the pattern on log house prices: p = 0.10, 0.43 and 0.78 for the first
three, p ≈ 0 for Hadri.

**Lag length.** Every test except Hadri needs the $p_i$ lags of the ADF
regression. `purtest` fixes them by hand or chooses them per unit by AIC, SIC,
or the general-to-specific rule of @hall1994. Too few lags leave serial
correlation in $\varepsilon_{it}$ and over-reject. Too many waste the short *T*
the panel was meant to compensate for.

## 3. First and second generation: one assumption

"Second generation" is not a date. It is one assumption dropped: that units
are independent once a common time effect is removed.

The first generation allows exactly one form of dependence. Subtract the
cross-section mean each period and a common shock that hits every unit
*equally* disappears. That is the two-way fixed-effects identity of
[cross-sectional
dependence](../02-cross-dependence/theory-cross-sectional-dependence.qmd):
a time effect is a factor model with every loading equal to one. If the
loadings differ, demeaning leaves the factor in the residuals and every
unit's evidence is partly the same evidence.

Pesaran's CADF regression [@pesaran2007] allows heterogeneous loadings. It
adds the cross-section averages $\bar y_{t-1}$ and $\Delta \bar y_t$ to each
unit's ADF equation:

$$\Delta y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i y_{i,t-1} + c_i \bar y_{t-1}
  + d_i \Delta \bar y_t + \dots + e_{it}.$$

The averages proxy the single unobserved factor, and each unit gets its own
coefficients on them, so each unit gets its own loading. CIPS is the mean of
the resulting *t* statistics — IPS on defactored regressions
[@baltagi2021, pp. 352–353]. The idea is the same one that drives CCE
estimation, in [common factors and
CCE](../02-cross-dependence/theory-common-factors-cce.qmd).

`plm::cipstest` exposes all three levels of this argument through `model`:

| `model =` | Regression | Handles |
|---|---|---|
| `"mg"` | plain ADF per unit, averaged | independence only — this is IPS |
| `"dmg"` | ADF on cross-sectionally demeaned data | one factor, equal loadings |
| `"cmg"` (default) | CADF, with cross-section averages | one factor, any loadings |

Nothing in **plm** handles more than one factor. @pesaran2013 extend CIPS by
adding further cross-section averages of other variables, and add the CSB
statistic [@pesaran2015, p. 836]. Moon–Perron [@moon2004], Bai–Ng's PANIC
[@bai2004] and Phillips–Sul [@phillips2003] defactor by principal components
first and test afterwards. None has an R implementation in this project.

CIPS has a cost: its distribution is non-standard and depends on *N*, *T* and
the deterministic terms. `cipstest` returns the nearest tabulated significance
level, not an exact p-value. A printed `p-value = 0.1` means *above* 0.10, and
`0.01` means *below* 0.01.

## 4. Size before power

Every comparative ranking of these tests in the textbooks is a ranking of
*power* — and power only means something when the test rejects a true null at
its nominal rate. Both standard rankings assume that:

- LLC has higher local power than IPS [@pesaran2015, p. 819];
- LLC and Breitung have the smallest size distortions, and Fisher does at
  least as well as IPS [@pesaran2015, p. 838; @baltagi2021, p. 348].

Two things break size in a large-*N*, short-*T* panel, and they compound.

**The shape of the panel.** LLC's asymptotics need *T* to grow faster than *N*
[@levin2002; @baltagi2021, pp. 340–343]. On independent random walks, with no
dependence at all, the
[examples' simulation](index.qmd#sec-ur-spatial-size) gives LLC a size
of 0.09 at N/T = 0.04 and 0.855 at N/T = 3.33. IPS is better but not right:
0.085 to 0.15 at T = 30. The target shape of this project is N/T ≈ 8.5, off
the end of that table.

**Cross-sectional dependence.** When units move together, *N* series are worth
fewer than *N* independent ones, and a test that counts them as *N*
over-rejects. @baltagi2007 ran 1600 experiments under spatial error
dependence: distortions are largest under a spatial autoregressive error and
grow with the density of W [@baltagi2021, pp. 353–354].

@pesaran2015 [p. 839] draws two rules from that literature, and they pull in
opposite directions:

- The CD-based approach (CIPS) is the most robust to spatial alternatives.
- Factor-based corrections are *invalid* under weak dependence, because they
  remove a "factor" that is not there.

In the project's own simulation, on a 7 × 7 rook W, CIPS held its size: 0.04
at λ = 0 and 0.07 at λ = 0.8. The four first-generation tests rejected a true
null two and a half to twelve times too often even at λ = 0. Shape, not space,
did most of the damage.

::: {.callout-warning}
**At N/T ≫ 1, a first-generation rejection is not evidence.** It is what those
tests do to random walks at that shape. Report CIPS, and read every
first-generation p-value as an upper bound on the evidence rather than a
measurement of it.
:::

## 5. What a rejection licenses

Under H₁b, a rejection means *some* share of units is stationary. It does not
say which, and it is not a licence to treat the panel as stationary and pool
it.

@hanck2013 turns the rejection into a list. Take the individual p-values a
Fisher-type test already computes, sort them, and apply two classical
multiple-testing results:

- **Simes' test** [@simes1986] of the intersection null. With sorted p-values
  $p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(N)}$, reject when
  $\min_j N p_{(j)}/j \le \alpha$. Unlike the Fisher combination, it stays
  valid under general cross-sectional dependence.
- **Hommel's procedure** [@hommel1988] for the individual hypotheses. It
  controls the family-wise error rate, so each unit is judged on its own
  without the multiplicity of *N* tests inflating false rejections.

`plm::phansitest` implements both. It accepts any `purtest` object with
per-series p-values (`madwu`, `Pm`, `invnormal`, `logit`, `ips`) and refuses
Hadri, whose statistic is not built from individual p-values.

The two cases in the examples show both outcomes:

| Panel | Simes global p | Units rejected (Hommel) |
|---|---|---|
| 19 real exchange rates [@hanck2013, Table 11] | 0.0003 | 10 of 19 |
| 49 US state house prices | 0.12 | 0 of 49 |

The exchange-rate panel rejects the intersection null *and* names the ten
stationary countries — the two answers Remark 8 asks for. The house-price
panel rejects neither. Note that its Simes p-value of 0.12 is far sharper than
the Maddala–Wu p-value of 0.43 on the same data.

## 6. The assumption no test checks

Cross-sectional *correlation* is units moving together. Cross-unit
*cointegration* is stronger: a linear combination of different units' series is
stationary, so the units share a stochastic trend. @pesaran2015 [p. 836]
warns that panel unit-root tests may be "severely biased" under the second
while tolerating the first.

CADF allows one common I(1) factor — that is what the cross-section averages
absorb — and rules out further cointegration among what is left
[@pesaran2015, p. 837]. The subsampling test of @choi2007 allows it but needs
*N* small relative to *T* [@pesaran2015, p. 838], the opposite of a spatial
panel.

Correlation does not reveal it. In the
[examples](index.qmd#sec-ur-cross-coint), a cointegrated pair and a
pair with correlated increments have correlations of 0.90 and 0.77. A
Johansen rank test separates them perfectly; no CD statistic or α could. So
every CIPS result in this book holds under an assumption the book cannot test.

## 7. If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| CD rejects, or α is near 1 | First-generation tests are invalid. Use CIPS. |
| N/T well above 1 | First-generation size is broken even without dependence. Use CIPS. |
| CIPS rejects | A share of units is stationary (H₁b). Name them with `phansitest`. |
| CIPS does not reject | Treat the panel as I(1). Corroborate with Hadri's reversed null. |
| Dependence is weak and spatial, not factor-driven | CIPS defactors needlessly. Its size survived λ ≤ 0.8 here, but that is not a general licence. |
| Several common factors are plausible | Not testable in this book. State it as a limitation. |
| The text says "the panel is stationary" | Rewrite it. Say which alternative was tested, and how many units. |

## 8. Open

- **Missing tests.** Breitung and Harris–Tzavalis — the two tests with the
  best size record in the comparisons — are not in `purtest`. The benchmark
  is Stata's `xtunitroot`.
- **Several factors.** CIPS with multiple factors and CSB [@pesaran2013],
  Moon–Perron and PANIC have no R implementation and no verification target.
- **Cross-unit cointegration.** No panel test exists in R. The assumption has
  to be carried as a stated limitation into Stage 2 of
  `.docs/panel-spat-PLAN.md`.
- **The target shape.** No published size table covers N ≈ 170, T ≈ 20 with a
  spatial W. The examples' Monte Carlo is the only evidence, and it covers
  this code on one W.
- **A software trap.** In **plm** 2.6.7, the print method of `phansitest`
  says "H0 rejected (globally)" whatever the result. Read `$rejected.no` and
  compute Simes' p-value directly.

## Next

With the unit-root question settled for a panel, the next one is whether its
I(1) series are cointegrated. That is Stage 2 of `.docs/panel-spat-PLAN.md`,
where the only verifiable route is the CCE-plus-CIPS substitute of
[the second-generation section](index.qmd#sec-ur-second-gen).
